ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: The pedigree chart of a family with two single-gene genetic diseases, A and B, is shown in the figure. Disease A is a certain familial hereditary tumor, controlled by alleles A/a; disease B is phenylketonuria, caused by a lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase, controlled by alleles B/b, and the two pairs of genes are inherited independently. Researchers performed PCR amplification on the two genes of members of this family, and the gel electrophoresis chart of amplification products of some members is shown in the figure. Analyze according to the figure, if Ⅲ-5 and Ⅲ-3 marry, what is the probability of giving birth to an affected child?

Disease A is a certain familial hereditary tumor, controlled by alleles A/a; disease B is phenylketonuria, caused by a lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase, controlled by alleles B/b, and the two pairs of genes are inherited independently. Researchers performed PCR amplification on the two genes of members of this family, and the gel electrophoresis chart of amplification products of some members is shown in the figure. Analyze according to the figure, if Ⅲ-5 and Ⅲ-3 marry, what is the probability of giving birth to an affected child?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the pedigree chart, Ⅰ-1 is a female with disease A, and Ⅰ-2 is a male with disease A; among the offspring of the two, Ⅱ-2 is a female with both disease A and disease B, while Ⅱ-3 and Ⅱ-5 appear normal. Ⅱ-3 and normal male Ⅱ-4 have a normal male Ⅲ-3; Ⅱ-5 and normal female Ⅱ-6 have a normal female Ⅲ-5. In the gel electrophoresis chart, Ⅰ-1 and Ⅰ-2 show double bands in the corresponding detection of the B/b gene, indicating that they are Bb; Ⅱ-4 and Ⅱ-6 are normal homozygous single bands in the corresponding detection of the B/b gene, and can be judged as BB. Then reason: In terms of disease A, Ⅰ-1 and Ⅰ-2 both have disease A but have normal offspring Ⅱ-3 and Ⅱ-5, indicating that disease A is autosomal dominant inheritance, and the genotype of normal persons is aa. Therefore Ⅱ-3 and Ⅱ-5 are both aa, and their offspring Ⅲ-3 and Ⅲ-5 also cannot carry the dominant pathogenic gene A, so the probability that the offspring of the two have disease A is 0. In terms of disease B, phenylketonuria is a recessive genetic disease, and the affected genotype is bb. Ⅰ-1 and Ⅰ-2 do not have disease B but have offspring with disease B, and electrophoresis shows that the two are Bb, so Ⅱ-3 and Ⅱ-5, as unaffected offspring of Bb×Bb, each have a probability of 2/3 of being carrier Bb. Ⅱ-4 and Ⅱ-6 are BB, therefore the probability that Ⅲ-3 is Bb is (2/3)×(1/2)=1/3, and the probability that Ⅲ-5 is Bb is also 1/3. If Ⅲ-3 and Ⅲ-5 marry, only when both are Bb is it possible to give birth to a child with disease B, with probability (1/3)×(1/3)×(1/4)=1/36. Since the risk of disease A is 0, the total probability of giving birth to an affected child is 1/36.
